blocks.text: The Martin Parr Foundation presents “Dark Tales: British Documentary and the Gothic,” an exhibition that reminds the viewer what makes an atmosphere distinctively British: a fondness for dark irony, layered emotional depth, and a passion for the absurd.
By Gaia Squarci. Cover Photo by Chris Shaw

blocks.caption: Conservative Party fundraiser, England, 1988. © Martin Parr _ Magnum Photos

blocks.text: Curator Isaac Blease drew the selection from over 5,000 prints in the Foundation’s collection, spanning more than 80 years, from the post-war years to the present. Together they build a haunted, playful narrative that shows photography’s power to visualise fear and fascination — proof, as Blease puts it, of the Gothic principle that horror lives closest to the familiar.

blocks.caption: ‘Sunderland, North East of England 1962’. Coal scavengers working on a mound. Part of the grafters collection. © Colin Jones/TopFoto
Window of Hill’s Gents Tailoring. Covent Garden, London. October 22, 1986. © Jim Dow

blocks.text: Rather than impose a single viewpoint, the show lets atmosphere serve as its thread, moving from historical documentation to domestic unease to class, into the rituals of appearance and respectability, where details of style are always an indicator of a deeper message. Fading industrial towns, claustrophobic interiors, and eerie nocturnal scenes recur throughout, in work by Bill Brandt, Anna Fox, Don McCullin, Lee Miller, Chris Shaw, and many others.

blocks.caption: Derry_Londonderry, Northern Ireland, at around 4 PM on August 12, 1969. © estate of Akihiko Okamura
‘Shelter from the Heat’, Shelton Bar Steelworks, Stoke-on-Trent, 1978. © Janine Wiedel.jpg

blocks.text: The exhibition “Dark Tales: British Documentary and the Gothic” is on view at the Martin Parr Foundation in Bristol, UK, until December 20.
